children: Chicago wheat futures fell on Wednesday, retreating from multi-year highs hit in the previous session as traders considered the latest developments affecting Black Sea grain exports, while corn and soybeans also dropped.
The most traded wheat contract on the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT)
was down 1.34% at $7.72 a bushel by 1045 GMT. CBOT corn
lost 1.42% to $5.38-1/4 a bushel while soybeans
fell 1% to $13.04-1/4 a bushel.

Wheat had reached its highest in three and a half years on Tuesday after reports that Moscow had rejected a moratorium on attacks in the Black Sea region and struck port infrastructure overnight in its ongoing conflict with Ukraine.
"The physical disruption remains serious, but the market is now carrying a substantial war-risk premium and speculative length," CM Navigator analysts said in a note.
"That sensitivity is already visible this morning, with CBOT wheat, corn and beans giving back part of yesterday's gains despite another overnight attack on Odesa."
Russia attacked Ukraine's port infrastructure and a border crossing with Romania in the southern Black Sea region of Odesa the previous night, Ukrainian officials said.
Ukraine's largest farm union UAC warned exporters on Wednesday not to expect deep-water ports to resume operations soon and to rely on available alternatives.
Meanwhile, Turkey's President Tayyip Erdogan said that a mechanism was needed to ensure permanent safety of commercial maritime transport in the Black Sea before a grain crisis escalates.
For corn, the U.S. Department of Agriculture kept its good-to-excellent rating for the American corn crop unchanged at 57% in a weekly report on Monday. That was down from 69% a year ago.
Crops were drying down before harvesting in the Midwest, with hot and dry weather expected over the next week.
For soybeans, uncertainty over U.S. yield potential supported prices after the USDA lowered its condition rating for the nation's soybean crop on Monday.

Brazil's 2026/27 soybean crop is expected to reach a record 183.5 million metric tons, brokerage and consultancy StoneX said on Tuesday, raising its estimate from an August forecast of 183.1 million tons.
